t: Executive Order 14318 speeds federal permitting for big data centers
b: Covers projects adding more than 100 MW of load or committing at least $500 million. Directs agencies to streamline environmental review, offer federal sites (DOE labs, Air Force bases), and find brownfield and Superfund land. It does not override state or local zoning, which is where most permits live.
iw: Faster federal review and federal sites, though local permits still decide most projects

t: DOE orders FERC to write the first federal rules for connecting large loads
b: Using a rarely invoked Section 403 power, Energy Secretary Wright proposed a 20 MW threshold, standardized study deposits, and assigning all network upgrade costs to the load. State utility regulators objected that load interconnection has always been state turf. The docket (RM26-4) remains open.
iw: Could speed grid hookups but would assign all upgrade costs to the data center

t: Order directs Commerce to list state AI laws it considers invalid
b: Executive Order 14365 gave Commerce 90 days to publish an evaluation of "onerous" state AI laws. Potentially relevant to state data center rules, but the evaluation was not public when the March 11 deadline passed, and law firm reviews through the summer found it still unpublished.
iw: A published list could be used to challenge state rules

t: Ratepayer Protection Pledge: seven tech companies promise to pay for new power
b: Google, Microsoft, Meta, Oracle, xAI, OpenAI and Amazon committed to cover new generation and grid upgrades for their data centers. The pledge is voluntary and has no enforcement mechanism. In July the White House said more than 200 utilities, developers, cooperatives and states had joined.
iw: Adds cost voluntarily, but buys political cover and heads off mandates

t: AI Data Center Moratorium Act (S.4214 / H.R.9442)
b: Sanders introduced it in March and Ocasio-Cortez filed the House version in June. It would halt construction or expansion of AI data centers over 20 MW until Congress passes safeguards on AI safety, power prices, labor and the environment. Referred to committee; widely seen as unlikely to pass, and Sen. Warner publicly rejected the idea.
iw: Would halt large AI facilities nationwide, though passage is unlikely

t: First data center gets FAST-41 covered-project status
b: Puts a data center on the federal fast-track permitting dashboard for the first time.
iw: Federal fast-track review for a project

t: EPA proposes letting construction start before air permits
b: Revises Clean Air Act New Source Review definitions so developers can do significant site work, down to concrete pads, before getting a preconstruction permit. The agency cited the data center order. Environmental groups say it removes an early check on gas-fired projects.
iw: Lets site work begin before air permits, cutting months off schedules

t: FERC tells all six grid operators to fix or justify large-load rules
b: Instead of a national rule, FERC issued show-cause orders to PJM, MISO, SPP, CAISO, ISO-NE and NYISO. Each had to file an informational report within 30 days and a response by Aug 17, covering cost recovery from large loads, co-location and new transmission services. Regional rules are being written now.
iw: Faster connection options, paired with stricter cost recovery and credit rules

t: Pledge expands to 23 Republican governors and 187 companies
b: Utilities including NextEra, Duke, AEP, Southern and PG&E joined, along with developers such as Equinix and Digital Realty. The White House says signers deliver 80% of U.S. power. Still voluntary; enforcement depends on state utility commissions. Democratic governors Moore and Shapiro said they were not invited.
iw: Voluntary cost commitments; more signers means more pressure to deliver

t: EPA moves to ease rules for on-site gas power and narrow public comment
b: Reported proposals would treat some temporary turbines as mobile equipment and drop federal public-participation requirements for minor-source permits. Separate guidance says off-grid power plants generally fall outside the Acid Rain Program. Environmental groups allege some developers already split projects to qualify as minor sources.
iw: Eases on-site gas power and narrows public challenges

t: GRID Savings Act offered as the Democratic alternative
b: Sen. Heinrich's bill would direct federal regulators to require large customers to pay for the grid upgrades and connection facilities they need, rather than asking states to consider it. Schumer and others point to it and to Van Hollen's bill as the binding version.
iw: Would make paying full grid costs mandatory

t: Ratepayer Protection Act passes House 417–3, stalls in Senate 57–43
b: Would require state utility regulators to consider standards making large loads pay the full incremental cost of serving them. It does not require states to adopt them, which is why Senate Democrats called it a messaging bill. Ossoff, Warnock, Hassan and Klobuchar crossed over. The White House said Trump would have signed it. Senators say a bipartisan permitting bill unveiled the same day carries a similar provision.
iw: Failure leaves cost rules to states; no federal mandate either way

t: Energize NY Development proceeding on large-load interconnection
b: The PSC opened Case 26-E-0045 on how big loads connect and who pays. NYISO's large-load queue grew from about 1 GW in 2022 to roughly 12 GW by the end of 2025.
iw: Likely to push more interconnection costs onto large loads

t: Responsible Data Center Development Act (S10642/A11560) awaits Hochul
b: Passed 44–16 and 102–39. One-year pause on state environmental permits for data centers of 20 MW and up, separate electric and water rate classes, renewable targets for 5 MW+ facilities (one-third by 2030, 90% by 2040), labor standards and public hearings. Hochul has until Dec 31 to sign or veto; if she does nothing, it dies.
iw: Pause plus rate classes, renewable mandates and labor rules

t: Executive Order 62: first statewide data center pause
b: Freezes discretionary state environmental approvals for new data centers of 50 MW or more for up to a year while the Department of Public Service prepares a generic environmental impact statement. Excludes projects with complete applications, ministerial permits, and local approvals. Also asks regulators to weigh a grid fund paid by large loads and to repeal sales tax breaks.
iw: Freezes state approvals for large projects for up to a year

t: Abbott freezes new grid approvals pending an ERCOT audit
b: Orders ERCOT and the PUC to audit every data center in the interconnection queue (tax breaks, power source, water, community impacts, ownership) before any advance. ERCOT paused its Batch Zero study. The queue holds about 474 GW, roughly 90% data centers. ERCOT says the review runs to December. At least 43 companies publicly backed the audit.
iw: Freezes grid approvals in the hottest market; about 50 GW exposed

t: Water board told to penalize data centers that skip its survey
b: As few as 28% of data centers had answered a state water-use survey. Nonresponders can now face civil and criminal liability and lose state permits. A progress report was due Oct 14.
iw: New reporting duties backed by permit penalties

t: TCEQ ordered to issue no data center permits until audits finish
b: Closes the behind-the-meter gap: projects that build their own power and skip the grid queue still need state environmental permits. TCEQ reports back by Oct 19. Abbott also says he will ask the 2027 legislature to eliminate data center incentives. His opponent calls the pause a scam she expects to end after the election.
iw: Halts state permits, closing the self-powered workaround

t: Virginia signs its energy and data center bills, including HB 1393 / SB 253
b: Of 61 data center bills, 15 reached the governor; 46 carry over to 2027. Facilities of 25 MW and up pay for added generating capacity. Spanberger amended the cost bill to tell regulators to make sure other customers are not subsidizing data centers. Other bills tighten backup generator and water rules and give localities more review tools.
iw: Higher cost responsibility for 25 MW+ loads and more local review

t: Budget creates a tax on data center electricity use
b: A $0.011 per kWh consumption tax from July 1, 2026 through June 30, 2028, capped at $600 million a year with any excess refunded. The equipment sales tax exemption, worth an estimated $1.6 to $1.9 billion a year, survives. Senate leader Lucas says she will keep pushing for repeal; the industry's trade group says Virginia broke its word.
iw: New operating cost, though the larger sales tax break survived

t: Regulators make data centers pay for transmission built only for them
b: Followed a filing by the governor's office urging the change. The administration projects savings of hundreds of millions of dollars for other customers.
iw: Dedicated transmission now billed to the data center

t: California signs seven data center laws
b: AB 1577 (energy and noise reporting), AB 2383 and SB 886 (dedicated tariffs and full upgrade costs, tariffs due by Jan 1, 2028), AB 2469 and AB 2619 (water supply assessments and water reporting tied to permits and licenses), SB 887 (no CEQA categorical exemptions) and SB 1168 (rate design study). No moratorium. Most provisions take effect Jan 1, 2027.
iw: Higher grid costs, water and disclosure duties, no ban

t: Executive Order 2026-05 makes GRID standards binding
b: Projects of 25 MW and up must sign a consent order committing to full grid cost responsibility, new in-state generation with rising clean-firm shares (10% in 2027 to 32% by 2035), disclosure and community benefits, or face slower review. No state permit issues without local approval. Removes data centers from fast-track permitting, bans agency NDAs and ties the sales tax exemption to compliance. Senate Republicans called it a political reversal.
iw: Binding cost, clean-energy and local-approval conditions

t: House committees advance HB 2775, HB 2828 and HB 2674 unanimously
b: The Energy Committee passed HB 2775 (apply and pay for grid interconnection before seeking local zoning) and HB 2828 (data centers bear generation and grid-upgrade costs). The Consumer Protection committee passed HB 2674, barring data centers from claiming public utility status to override zoning or use eminent domain.
iw: Would codify cost responsibility and limit utility status claims

t: SB 135 and HB 1038, a "Data Center Bill of Rights"
b: Instead of a statewide ban, the state requires data centers of 10 MW and up to pay for rate increases they cause, adds water-use rules, and bars the state from preempting local ordinances, so counties and towns can regulate or prohibit data centers.
iw: Gives every county and town the power to say no

t: HB 1210 shares data center tax savings with local governments
b: Data centers receiving the state sales tax exemption must pass 1% of those savings to local governments.
iw: Small revenue share in exchange for keeping the exemption

t: Mills vetoes LD 307, which would have paused data centers until late 2027
b: The bill would have stopped applications for data centers over 20 MW. Mills said a pause was appropriate in principle but objected that it would block a locally backed project in Jay. The override attempt fell short.
iw: Blocked what would have been the first statutory statewide pause

t: Florida law aims to keep data center costs off household bills
b: Signed in May; DeSantis said it prevents utilities from passing data center energy costs to residential and small business customers. He was one of three Republican governors who did not sign the White House pledge.
iw: Costs can no longer be spread to household bills

t: Executive Order 26-058 ties the tax exemption to a protection framework
b: Louisiana Economic Development must build a Ratepayer and Community Protection Framework; companies must attest to compliance to keep the sales and use tax exemption.
iw: Tax break now comes with compliance attestations

t: Executive Order 26-17 creates a data center task force
b: Studies water and environmental impacts and drafts county zoning guidelines, with recommendations to lawmakers by 2027.
iw: Study only for now; rules may follow in 2027

t: Oregon pauses state land transactions for data centers
b: Runs through July 1, 2027. Applies to state-owned land, not a general construction ban. Builds on the 2025 POWER Act, which gave facilities of 20 MW and up their own rate class.
iw: Closes state-owned land to new projects until mid-2027

t: Executive order requires community benefits agreements before state permits
b: Executive Order 658 bars state permits for data centers over 25 MW without a community benefits agreement meeting state standards, bans NDAs with state agencies, and makes projects without their own clean power pay into a ratepayer fund.
iw: Adds a local negotiation step before state permits

t: Ayotte plans a multi-year statewide moratorium in her next budget
b: A Republican governor proposing a statewide pause, announced after news of a possible hyperscale site at the former Bow coal plant. It would go in the budget trailer bill and take effect no sooner than July 2027; Democrat Cinde Warmington says she would impose one by executive order on day one.
iw: Signals a possible multi-year statewide pause

t: Task force to review every data center of 25 MW or more seeking state action
b: Projects need a public "aligned" finding to get state incentives, and agencies defer permits until local approvals are in hand. Moore also wants the 2020 sales tax exemption repealed; a statewide moratorium bill, HB 120, died in committee.
iw: Extra state review for every large project

t: Pritzker announces a two-year suspension of incentives for new projects
b: Announced in February. He has since said he will not pursue a statewide moratorium and wants tougher rules from lawmakers in 2027.
iw: Suspends incentives for new projects

t: Georgia's session ends with data center limits unpassed
b: HB 1059 died in committee. SB 476, which would have ended most state tax credits including those for data centers, passed the Senate in February. Georgia Power's plans show data centers driving most new capacity.
iw: Limits died and incentives remain intact

t: Statewide moratorium bills mostly stall
b: Bills were filed in at least a dozen states, including Georgia, Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, New Hampshire, Oklahoma, South Carolina, South Dakota, Vermont, Virginia and Wisconsin. Maine's passed and was vetoed; New York's passed and awaits the governor. Executive orders, not statutes, produced the pauses now in force.
iw: Most statewide pause bills failed

t: Statewide ban amendment misses 2026 ballot, retargets 2027
b: Would bar new data centers drawing more than 25 MW. Volunteers had about 70,000 of 413,488 required signatures by July 1. Signatures do not expire in Ohio; the group reported 130,000+ by September and is aiming for November 2027.
iw: Statewide ban delayed at least a year

t: Ohio bills on NDAs, tariffs and incentives
b: HB 695 would ban NDAs between local officials and developers; HB 706 would extend AEP Ohio's data center tariff statewide; HB 710 would end incentives and eminent domain for data centers; HB 646, a study commission, passed the House unanimously. Gov. DeWine had earlier vetoed data center provisions in the budget.
iw: Would raise costs and limit incentives and secrecy

t: 7–0 vote halts new data centers through Jan 31, 2028
b: Softened from an outright ban into a pause on new applications until Jan. 31, 2028, or until comprehensive rules pass. Projects already in development and expansions of existing campuses can continue.
iw: Long countywide halt in a key East Coast market

t: One-year moratorium on large data centers
b: Mayor Brandon Scott signed a one-year pause on data centers projected to use 10 MW or more, proposed by Council President Zeke Cohen. It also orders a city study of energy, infrastructure and job effects.
iw: Citywide pause on large facilities

t: Protests erupt as Memphis council delays its moratorium vote
b: Police cleared the chamber after a 7–5 vote to postpone the decision two weeks. The council later rejected an 18-month pause and passed a 135-day one.
iw: Visible opposition in a major hub

t: First Texas city to exclude data centers from every zoning district
b: Passed 4–3. Earlier, Hill County adopted a county moratorium and rescinded it after a developer sued for $100 million. State lawmakers have since moved to limit city bans.
iw: Excludes data centers from every zone in a Texas city

t: Court sets aside county moratorium
b: Supervisors had extended a June pause in July. A judge found the county hadn't shown the immediate threat state law requires and directed it be set aside. The county said it would bring a new moratorium.
iw: A court lifted a local pause

t: 120-day pause in unincorporated areas
b: Passed 3–2. It covers projects that had not yet filed permits, so Project Blue and the proposed Project Gravel are exempt.
iw: Short pause, and the marquee projects are exempt

t: Six-month moratorium
b: The first on Georgia's coast, it covers unincorporated areas only. A rezoning request for a Kingsland-area industrial park that could have hosted data centers was withdrawn the day before.
iw: Nine-month local pause

t: One-year moratorium at a former steel plant site
b: The city hosts a proposed 100 MW project. Nearby, Mason repealed a permissive ordinance to write stricter rules.
iw: Year-long pause on a 100 MW site

t: Voters reject a data center rezoning, about 90% no
b: The township had changed farm and residential land to industrial for a proposed data center; voters overturned it.
iw: Voters killed the rezoning outright

t: Voters require a public vote on big incentive deals
b: About 66% approved requiring a vote before the city approves economic development deals over $10 million, such as data centers.
iw: Large incentive deals now need a public vote

t: About 20 local data center measures on the November ballot
b: Includes bans above power thresholds (25 MW in Pataskala, Sunbury and Granville; 7.5 MW in Urbana), outright prohibitions, and referendums on rezonings such as four in Wilmington. At least 125 local moratoriums are already in effect across Ohio. The Ohio Supreme Court has ruled on several petition disputes.
iw: Many bans and project referendums at once

t: Kansas towns vote on some of the strictest bans
b: Emporia would bar data centers over 10 MW or drawing 100,000 gallons a day in every zone; a judge ordered it onto the ballot, but the city's court challenge is pending. El Dorado votes on a 10-year ban on large data centers and battery storage.
iw: Some of the strictest thresholds anywhere (10 MW)

t: Advisory votes on data center development
b: Non-binding questions, four of them in Madison County, some proceeding even where officials already restricted data centers.
iw: Advisory only, but signals local opposition

t: Charter amendment to ban new data centers
b: Charter Amendment 4 would write the city's Sept. 14 ban into the charter, so only another referendum could undo it. The council voted unanimously Aug. 3 to put it on the ballot.
iw: Would lock a ban into the city charter

t: Vote on allowing data centers in the Eldorado Valley
b: One of the few measures that would permit development. Residents grew more vocal after a federal land approval for a project came without local input.
iw: Would open land to development if it passes

t: Voter approval for redevelopment of the old GM site
b: Would require a public vote before the city approves deals on the former GM/JATCO property when costs exceed $450 million.
iw: Adds a public vote before large deals

t: Measure to prohibit data centers citywide
b: Neighboring Monterey Park put its own ban to voters in June after a fight over diesel generators and noise.
iw: Would ban data centers citywide

t: Pause on new data center permits through end of 2027
b: The City-County Council voted 23–1 on Aug. 10 and the Metropolitan Development Commission gave final approval Aug. 19. Three already-approved projects, including Sabey's and DC Blox's, are exempt.
iw: Major metro paused through 2027

t: Pause on new applications until May 2027
b: The council voted unanimously for a one-year pause on new data center zoning permits and site plans while a working group drafts rules. CoreSite's building under construction is exempt, but its two planned additions are blocked.
iw: Pause until new city rules are written

t: A wave of town moratoriums
b: Chelsea adopted a one-year pause in July. In August Pinson (one year), Harpersville and Westover (six months) and Anniston (12 months) followed, and Prichard approved six months amid a data center plan there. Foley added six months Sept. 8.
iw: Many small pauses add up across a region

t: Cherokee Nation bars large data centers on tribal lands
b: Hyperscale data centers are banned on tribally owned and trust land after 64% of surveyed citizens opposed them; projects elsewhere on the reservation need robust consultation. It followed a Seminole Nation moratorium.
iw: Bars large data centers on tribal lands

t: Three-year moratorium through October 2029
b: Citizens voted 261–83 at the annual Tribal Council meeting to bar data center construction on tribal lands, despite Gov. Reggie Wassana's case for development.
iw: Three-year halt on tribal lands

t: Ramaswamy promises a day-one order halting new data center approvals
b: The Republican governor nominee says the pause would last until lawmakers pass his Ohioans-First law, which would require data centers to give free electricity to nearby residents. He went further than his Democratic opponent.
iw: Frontrunner-level candidate pledging an immediate statewide halt

t: Acton calls for a conditional statewide moratorium
b: The Democratic nominee asked the Statehouse to pass a conditional pause and attacked Ramaswamy as too close to tech billionaires.
iw: Conditional pause from the other major candidate

t: Ohio voters favor Brown over Husted by 11 points on data centers
b: The Senate race's weakest issue for the Republican incumbent, according to the poll.
iw: Shows opposing data centers wins votes

t: Leaked GOP memo calls data centers the anchor around Husted's neck
b: The Senate Republicans' campaign arm warned the issue had become a sleeper for the whole cycle.
iw: Even Republican strategists see the issue as a liability

t: Brown runs ads branding Husted the face of Ohio's data center boom
b: Brown blames Husted, who promoted projects as lieutenant governor, for higher bills and tax breaks. Husted's campaign says Brown's allies blocked his ratepayer bill.
iw: Anti-data center messaging is central to a top Senate race

t: Kaptur ads cast Merrin as "Data Center Derek" over Ohio's tax breaks
b: Kaptur's ads tie Merrin to his 2017 vote on the budget that widened Ohio's data center sales tax exemption; the Washington Reporter argues the vote was procedural. Merrin hasn't answered reporters' questions on data centers, and the toss-up race is drawing heavy outside spending.
iw: Data centers used as a campaign attack

t: Bresnahan and Cognetti campaign around data centers in northeast Pennsylvania
b: The district includes Archbald and Hazle Township, where multiple large proposals have drawn packed meetings and lawsuits.
iw: Industry becomes a House campaign issue

t: Garrity calls for a total pause on new data centers
b: The Republican nominee says a pause would let towns update zoning and set safeguards. Senate GOP leader Joe Pittman later cast Shapiro's executive order as a political reversal.
iw: Major-party nominee calling for a total pause

t: Hinojosa calls Abbott's data center pause a scam
b: The Democratic governor nominee wants an immediate moratorium and a special session to end tax breaks, and predicts Abbott will lift the pause after the election.
iw: Pressure to make the Texas pause tougher and longer

t: Texas agriculture commissioner calls Abbott's audit "all hat and no cattle"
b: Miller, a Republican, welcomed more scrutiny but says only laws with teeth will work and wants a special session.
iw: Republican pressure for binding laws

t: 43+ companies including Meta, OpenAI, Microsoft and AWS endorse Abbott's audit
b: Abbott's office touts the endorsements as proof the approach works; analysts question how much the audit will actually change.
iw: Industry cooperating to keep access to the Texas grid

t: Rally against data center development at the Texas Capitol
b: Protesters returned in September outside an industry event in downtown Austin.
iw: Visible grassroots opposition

t: Jolly backs a construction pause until Florida has a plan for water and the grid
b: The Democratic governor candidate joined a growing list of candidates in both parties calling for temporary halts.
iw: Candidate pledging a pause

t: Doug Jones says he would support a moratorium; Tuberville more supportive
b: Jones says Alabama shouldn't become a dumping ground because of lax zoning. Republican nominee Tommy Tuberville is friendlier to the industry.
iw: Pause pledge, though the GOP nominee is friendlier

t: Holscher, who voted for data center incentives, now backs a moratorium
b: The Democratic governor nominee says she would vote differently knowing what she knows now.
iw: Former supporter now backs a moratorium

t: Arizona's No Labels candidate promises a day-one moratorium
b: Part of a pattern of pause pledges by third-party and independent candidates, who lean more restrictive than major-party nominees.
iw: Candidate pledging a pause

t: Maryland's Republican nominee wants a moratorium
b: Adds to pressure on Gov. Moore, whose administration created a project review task force instead.
iw: Candidate pledging a pause

t: Benson calls for a data center moratorium until guardrails are in place
b: Her ad backs a pause until enforceable rules on water, power costs and union labor exist. Her husband works for Related Companies, developer of the Saline Township campus; Republican John James now opposes a statewide moratorium.
iw: Cost neutrality rather than a pause

t: Rob Sand: data centers shouldn't add a cent to Iowa bills
b: His plan would end Iowa's data center tax breaks, make developers cover all utility upgrade costs, bar NDAs and require public hearings. Republican nominee Zach Lahn has called for a moratorium.
iw: Cost neutrality rather than a pause

t: El-Sayed rallies at the Saline Township site, calls for no more approvals
b: The Senate candidate held the event outside the OpenAI and Oracle campus that broke ground two months earlier, saying approvals should stop until federal guardrails exist.
iw: Senate candidate calling for no more approvals

t: Kotek says Oregon needs to stop being a cheap date for data centers
b: She promised new safeguards but deferred specifics to her advisory committee, and at the time did not suggest stopping new data centers. Her focus was on tax breaks worth more than $400 million a year and on power costs; she later backed local moratoriums.
iw: Governor signaling tougher terms

t: Mazzei's conditions: local approval, self-supplied power, closed-loop cooling
b: The Republican nominee sets four terms instead of a pause: no taxpayer funding, their own electricity, locally approved industrial sites rather than farmland, and closed-loop cooling. Democrat Cyndi Munson promises a moratorium on her first day.
iw: New conditions on power, water and local approval

t: Georgia leads the country with nearly $13M in ads mentioning data centers
b: Two Public Service Commission seats that could flip the utility regulator are on the ballot.
iw: Heavy ad spending, mostly against data centers

t: Industry says Virginia is no longer a reliable partner
b: The trade group's president attacked the budget's consumption tax and rules; a clean energy group said the deal fell short from the other side.
iw: Industry pushback against new costs

t: Lucas vows to keep pushing to repeal the sales tax exemption
b: The Senate Finance chair, who led the repeal push, said the budget compromise does not end the fight.
iw: Continued push to end a $1.6B+ tax break

t: Virginians comfortable with a nearby data center fall from 69% to 35%
b: Comparison of 2023 and 2026 polling in the country's biggest data center market, as summarized by The Impact Project.
iw: Public support collapsing in the largest market

t: Trump criticizes Hochul's statewide pause
b: The president attacked the New York order shortly after it took effect, as Abbott was weighing his own pause.
iw: Presidential pressure against state pauses

t: Rally in Lansing presses Hochul to sign the legislative moratorium
b: About 200 people joined the bill's sponsors, part of a statewide tour of communities facing projects, including a proposed conversion of the old Cayuga power plant.
iw: Organized pressure for a statewide pause

t: Trump says towns rejecting data centers want to be "backwards and poor"
b: He added that China benefits from the backlash and warned opponents against killing the economy's golden goose.
iw: White House backing for development

t: Trump blames the radical left for trying to shut down development
b: At the pledge expansion event he said opponents would surrender the AI race to China. Environmental groups dismissed the pledge as unenforceable.
iw: White House backing for development

t: Schumer calls the Ratepayer Protection Act a fraud
b: He argued it leaves protections optional and urged votes on Van Hollen's and Heinrich's mandatory bills. Retiring Republican Thom Tillis agreed the bill wouldn't do much beyond messaging.
iw: Democrats want mandatory cost rules instead

t: Warner dismisses a federal moratorium as idiocy
b: The Virginia Democrat said a pause would only help China.
iw: A senior Democrat rejects a federal moratorium

t: OpenAI says China-linked accounts tried to stir up local opposition
b: The company said the debate is real but flagged a foreign influence attempt. Experts interviewed by Hearst stations say Trump overstates China's role relative to homegrown opposition.
iw: Gives industry a counter-narrative, but the opposition is mostly local

t: Nationwide day of protest against AI data center expansion
b: Demonstrations included New Port Richey, Florida.
iw: Visible grassroots opposition

t: About $130B in projects blocked or delayed in Q1; opposition groups top 800
b: The industry-adjacent tracker counted at least 75 projects stalled by local pushback and 833 active groups in 49 states.
iw: Opposition is already stalling projects at scale

t: BofA: pause proposals in 20 of 36 governor races
b: Analysts flag Texas as the largest risk, with about 50 GW of projects exposed, and expect capital to move toward states with clearer rules.
iw: Investors pricing in political risk

t: 30+ of 143 governor candidates back a pause, halt or ban
b: 20 Democrats and 10 Republicans. In five states (ME, NH, OH, OR, TX) both major-party candidates back a pause.
iw: Pause pledges spreading across both parties

t: At least 30 governor candidates back a data center pause, moratorium or ban
b: The Impact Project's count of 143 candidates in 36 states found 20 Democrats and 10 Republicans backing a pause; in Maine, New Hampshire, Ohio, Oregon and Texas, both major-party candidates do. Another 31 candidates are supportive, often with conditions.
iw: Pause pledges spreading across both parties

t: $45M spent on 2026 ads mentioning data centers, mostly against
b: Meanwhile Cleanview finds 75% of data centers under construction are in Republican-leaning states.
iw: Heavy ad spending, mostly against data centers

t: 71% oppose an AI data center in their area, 48% strongly
b: More than oppose a local nuclear plant. Opponents cite water and energy use, pollution and quality of life; supporters cite jobs and taxes.
iw: Majority opposition nationally

t: More oppose than favor local data centers, but few say they know much
b: Fielded June 2–4 among 2,023 adults.
iw: Majority opposition nationally

t: Opposition to nearby data centers jumps from 42% to 63% in eight months
b: Likely 2026 voters; 63% also say they are more concerned than excited about AI.
iw: Opposition rising quickly

t: 75% of voters now oppose a data center near them
b: Embold Research survey of 2,045 registered voters, Aug 8–13, continuing a slide since spring.
iw: Majority opposition nationally

t: 71% oppose AI data centers in their area; 52% back remote sites
b: 60% of voters view AI negatively overall.
iw: Majority opposition nationally

t: About 6 in 10 support limiting new data centers
b: 63% are concerned about the effect on electricity prices.
iw: Majority support for limits

t: 60% would be uncomfortable with a new data center nearby
b: Fielded July–August. An Annenberg survey found 61% opposition.
iw: Majority opposition nationally

t: 77% worry data centers will raise their electric rates
b: 64% said rapidly building data centers is not a good thing.
iw: Power-bill worries drive cost rules

t: Kotek pauses all state air and water permits for new data centers
b: A letter to the Department of Environmental Quality halts air and water discharge permits for new or expanded data centers until July 1, 2027, including pending applications and city wastewater permit changes. Reporters widely describe it as a de facto statewide moratorium. Projects already permitted can keep building.
iw: Without air or water permits, most large projects can't build until mid-2027

t: Executive Order 22 launches Virginia's Data Center Accountability Framework
b: Bans state agencies from signing nondisclosure agreements on data center projects, fast-tracks state noise rules, orders a review of diesel backup generator emissions, and designates Eastern Virginia a cooling-water-scarcity area. Most of the framework still needs legislation.
iw: More disclosure, noise and water scrutiny in the largest market

t: Arizona stops accepting new data center sales tax exemption applications until 2029
b: A provision in the budget Gov. Hobbs signed bars the Commerce Authority from taking new exemption applications from July 1, 2026 through June 30, 2029. Existing recipients keep their breaks. Developers filed 113 applications in the two weeks before the pause began.
iw: Three-year pause on a key incentive for new projects

t: SB 1359 would pause hyperscale data centers in Pennsylvania for three years
b: Would halt hyperscale projects that lack full approval, giving towns time to update their ordinances.
iw: Statewide pause proposal, unlikely to pass soon

t: Kotek and Drazan both now say they back a statewide moratorium
b: Kotek announced her support at a Salem rally on Sept. 8, and Drazan followed within hours. Each accuses the other of coming late to the position. An OPB-commissioned poll found nearly two-thirds of likely voters favor a temporary statewide ban, with the race a statistical tie.
iw: Both major candidates favor a statewide pause

t: Harford becomes the first Maryland county to ban data centers
b: The council passed Bill 26-011 7–0 as emergency legislation and County Executive Cassilly signed it the next day, prohibiting data centers in every zoning district. The Maryland Tech Council called the ban legally vulnerable.
iw: Permanent countywide ban

t: Baltimore County pauses data center permitting and orders a study
b: The council unanimously froze data center permits while the Planning Board studied impacts, with a report due Oct. 1. It later voted to extend the pause through December 2027.
iw: County permitting pause

t: Prince William ends by-right data center development countywide
b: Supervisors voted 8–0 to shrink the data center overlay district, so new projects outside it need a special use permit and a board vote. The same day they rejected Dominion's Vint Hill substation expansion.
iw: Slower, less certain path in a core Northern Virginia market

t: Supervisors reject the 2,000-acre Dulles Cloud South campus
b: An 8–0 vote denied the plan amendment for what would have been the county's largest project, about 43 million square feet near the Loudoun line. It came days after developers dropped their fight over the Digital Gateway complex.
iw: Largest proposed project in the county killed

t: Loudoun moves toward a 12-month pause on new data center applications
b: The heart of Data Center Alley voted to pause board action on legislative data center and some substation applications while it rewrites its rules. By-right projects continue. The final vote was deferred to Nov. 17.
iw: A pause in the world's densest data center market

t: Chesapeake limits data centers to conditional uses and bans groundwater use
b: The unanimous ordinance closes by-right loopholes, while an eight-month application pause remains in effect.
iw: Stricter review and water limits

t: Henry County adopts strict data center district rules
b: Adopted unanimously after residents pushed back at a July 28 hearing. Requires rezoning to a new district plus a special use permit, 1,000-foot setbacks from non-industrial land, a 50 dBA noise limit, limits on cooling technology and water-use studies. No land is zoned for it yet.
iw: Tough siting conditions

t: Hanover supervisors reject a 430-acre data center campus 4–3
b: Developer Tract sought rezoning for the Mountain Road Technology Park, which projected up to 2 million gallons of water a day at peak.
iw: Project denied

t: Frederick County weighs removing data centers from its zoning entirely
b: The planning commission unanimously recommended eliminating data centers as a permitted or conditional use in every district, after recommending denial of two proposals.
iw: Would amount to a countywide ban

t: Leon County adopts an 18-month data center moratorium
b: Commissioners unanimously paused review of large-load facilities, including data centers, after deciding a one-year pause wasn't long enough.
iw: Long countywide pause

t: Manatee County approves a 12-month data center moratorium
b: Ordinance 26-42 stops new data center applications in unincorporated areas. A state law effective July 1 preserves local planning authority over facilities of 50 MW and up.
iw: One-year county pause

t: Palm Beach County adopts a one-year pause on hyperscale data centers
b: Unanimous final vote, after multiple applications and this summer's rejection of Project Tango. Covers facilities of 50 MW or more, through September 2027.
iw: One-year county pause

t: Martin County advances a one-year moratorium; final vote Oct. 27
b: Passed unanimously on first reading. The county received a data center application the day before the hearing.
iw: Likely one-year county pause

t: Coweta County imposes a second 180-day data center moratorium
b: Unanimous. It halts permits, rezonings and hearings while the county revises its ordinance, but the five data centers already proposed have vested rights and are exempt. The county approved the $17 billion Project Sail campus 3–2 in April.
iw: Six-month county pause

t: Albany approves a 12-month data center moratorium
b: Unanimous, with an option to extend six months while planners and an outside consultant draft rules. Dougherty County had started a 45-day pause earlier in July.
iw: One-year city pause

t: Murray County extends its data center moratorium to July 2027
b: Sole Commissioner Noah Bishop turned a 90-day pause into a 12-month one, expiring July 7, 2027, citing a cyberattack that delayed drafting rules and uncertainty about large data centers.
iw: Year-long extension

t: Franklin County pauses data centers through 2028
b: Unanimous. The pause on data center special-use permits in unincorporated areas runs through Dec. 31, 2028, while the county updates its comprehensive plan, including wind and solar siting rules.
iw: Two-year-plus county pause

t: Savannah adopts a 155-day data center moratorium
b: Unanimous; it covers data centers of 10 MW or more and conversions of large industrial buildings, as OpenAI plans a 3.2 GW campus in neighboring Effingham County.
iw: City pause near a major new campus

t: Penn Township limits data centers to one small industrial district
b: Conditional use only, with noise caps, on-site power requirements and impact studies.
iw: Tight siting and power rules

t: East Whiteland adopts a 32-page data center ordinance after a moratorium
b: Sets distances from homes, schools and parks and covers noise, water, cooling and power. It doesn't affect the 1.5 million-square-foot project already under construction that sparked it.
iw: Stricter rules for future projects

t: Hazle Township pauses data center applications for 180 days
b: Aimed at Project Hazelnut, a proposed 15-building, 1,300-acre complex on a former coal plateau.
iw: Pause blocks a very large proposal

t: East Vincent rejects a 1.9 million-square-foot data center at Pennhurst
b: Supervisors unanimously denied the conditional use application at the historic state school site, finding it didn't meet zoning standards. The developer appealed to the Chester County Court of Common Pleas on June 26.
iw: Project denied

t: Milwaukee council votes 13–0 for a one-year data center moratorium
b: Bars new data centers and most expansions until the city writes zoning rules. Awaits the mayor's signature; he supports it. Madison, Dane County and Manitowoc County have adopted their own pauses.
iw: One-year pause in the state's largest city

t: Kalamazoo enacts a one-year data center moratorium
b: The commission unanimously stopped accepting data center, battery storage and crypto mining applications through Aug. 16, 2027, as a stopgap while zoning changes are drafted.
iw: City pause

t: Lansing adopts a 182-day pause on new data centers
b: Voted 7–1; runs from July 27 through Jan. 25, 2027. It followed Deep Green's withdrawal in April of a 24 MW downtown proposal.
iw: Six-month city pause

t: Flint votes 7–1 for a one-year data center moratorium
b: Adopted after more than 20 residents spoke against data centers amid talk of the former Buick City site. It also calls for an independent study.
iw: One-year city pause

t: Saginaw adopts permanent data center zoning
b: Voted 8–0. Data centers become special land uses in industrial districts with a 500-foot residential setback and a 55-decibel noise cap, effective Oct. 9; the city's moratorium runs through year-end.
iw: Rules rather than a pause

t: Ypsilanti utility halts water and sewer service to new data centers for a year
b: Prompted by a proposed $1.2 billion University of Michigan facility and a separate $1 billion proposal.
iw: No water means no new projects

t: Van Buren Township approves the site plan for Google's 1 GW campus
b: The planning commission voted 5–1, clearing the way for Michigan's second hyperscale facility near Detroit Metro Airport. Regulators approved its 20-year DTE power contract Oct. 1.
iw: Major project approved

t: Fort Wayne council defeats a one-year data center moratorium
b: The moratorium failed on a 4–4 tie and a study commission failed 3–5. Neither would have affected Google's operating southeast campus.
iw: Pause rejected

t: Michigan City weighs a new moratorium that exempts Google's project
b: Residents and the original sponsors object to the exemption for Project Maize. The pause could run to July 2028.
iw: Possible long pause, but the big project is exempt

t: Shelby County advances a moratorium for areas outside Memphis
b: Passed first reading 5–4 with four abstentions. Needs two more readings; some commissioners question the county's authority.
iw: Possible county pause

t: Nashville pauses data center permits until Dec. 1
b: Metro Council passed BL2026-1448 alongside zoning rules that ban the largest data centers. DC Blox's project next to the zoo filed for permits first, so the new rules likely don't apply to it.
iw: Pause in a major metro

t: Guilford County postpones a vote on a 180-day moratorium
b: After a long hearing where many speakers called six months too short, commissioners delayed the decision to their next meeting.
iw: Pause still likely

t: Orange County pauses large data centers for a year
b: Voted 6–0 to give staff time to rewrite land use policies before any applications arrive.
iw: One-year county pause

t: Lexington pauses data center permits and zone changes
b: Unanimous; runs to at least Oct. 31. A first reading of an extension was scheduled Oct. 8 while new zoning rules are drafted.
iw: City-county pause

t: Lowndes County approves agreements for Project Red Clay
b: Commissioners voted 3–2, a week before a scheduled special meeting, to approve development terms and a 20-year, $1.15 billion tax break for Cloverleaf's campus. Residents have since sued.
iw: Project approved with incentives

t: Monterey Park voters ban data centers in a landslide
b: Measure NDC, with about 87% support in early returns, permanently prohibits data centers within city limits. It grew out of opposition to a proposed 250,000 sq ft facility.
iw: Voter-approved permanent ban

t: Snohomish County imposes a six-month emergency pause
b: Covers new or expanded data centers of 2 MW or more in unincorporated areas, through Dec. 24 unless renewed.
iw: Low threshold catches small projects

t: Skamania County adopts a data center moratorium the day residents ask
b: Unanimous, though the county had no applications. Neighboring Klickitat County chose a policy statement instead.
iw: Preemptive county pause

t: Hillsboro adopts a 120-day data center moratorium
b: A major Oregon data center hub, acting before the state's permit pause.
iw: Short pause in an established hub
